title: Ives’s Missing Symphony — public composition log
scope: The log the composing agent (Claude) kept while writing this work: the request, its progress messages, the commands it ran on the score and their output, draft publications and test results, up to the publication step. It was written during the work, entry by entry; it is not an automatic export of the whole session, and the same session composed other works whose entries are not included here.
policy: Messages and tool output are recorded as they occurred, shortened where marked. Private internal reasoning, credentials, access details, private paths and unrelated conversation are not included. Statements made during the work may be provisional or mistaken; later corrections remain in the log.

entries.speaker: User
entries.text:
[A long batch brief was pasted: compose and publish one original symphony for each composer in the Missing Works catalogue who has no completed symphony, one composer at a time, claiming each open symphony request through the admin command, publishing live drafts early, testing every movement in the real browser player, writing a notebook and a public composition log, deploying an atomic release, and completing the request only after the public work is verified. Every work must be labelled an original AI-composed homage, with new thematic material rather than recognisable existing melodies.]

NOW I know I said to do all composers, but how about we actually do half of the composers in each section? just to save some money.

entries.speaker: Claude
entries.text:
Composition brief — Ives’s Missing Symphony (work id ives-symphony-1)

Charles Ives wrote four numbered symphonies. Their most personal feature is the use of hymns, marches and fiddle tunes that his listeners knew, quoted and piled on top of one another in different keys and speeds. A homage cannot do that honestly with real tunes here: this library asks for new thematic material, not recognisable existing melodies. So the first decision was to write three plain tunes of my own in those three manners — a hymn in F, a quickstep march in C and a fiddle tune in D — and then to treat them as Ives treated borrowed ones. Nothing is quoted from Ives or from any hymnal or march.

Orchestra (14 staves, sounding pitch): pairs of flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons, four horns, two trumpets, three trombones, timpani, tubular bells, strings.

Movements
I. Andante: the hymn, plainly, then with the same hymn following in another key, then with the march against it and bells; it breaks off and ends quietly on an open chord.
II. Allegro: the march; the fiddle tune enters in another key while the march’s bass keeps going; both bands at once; a sudden stop.
III. Largo: a very slow, very quiet string chorale that never changes; a horn asks the same five-note question five times; the woodwind answer four times, each time faster and more crowded, and the last question is left unanswered. The idea is that of “The Unanswered Question”; the notes are new.
IV. Finale: the hymn as a short fugato, then all three tunes together at full strength, a collapse, and a quiet close with the hymn far away and bells.

Target length about eight minutes. Because simultaneous keys are the point, the half-step and parallel-motion checks are switched off for this work; bar lengths, ranges, sustain and playback are still checked. Compromise known from the start: the tunes and their layering are written by hand; the plain string harmony under them is realised by a program from a chord plan.
